name: Martin Van Buren
role: Eighth president of the United States (1837-1841); earlier senator, governor of New York, secretary of state and vice president
summary: Van Buren was a Jacksonian Democrat who held that the federal government should keep to its enumerated powers, stay out of banking and private enterprise, and leave slavery alone where it existed. As president he opposed a national bank, proposed an independent treasury, carried out the removal of the Cherokee and kept to neutrality abroad. Late in life he stood for the Union against secession.

sources.title: Special Session Message, September 4, 1837
sources.author: Martin Van Buren, via Miller Center
sources.usedFor: Rejection of a national bank, the proposed divorce of the Treasury from banks, and his view that government should interfere as little as possible in private pursuits.

sources.title: Second Annual Message to Congress, December 3, 1838
sources.author: Martin Van Buren, via Miller Center
sources.usedFor: Reports the removal of the Cherokee and the purchase of Indian lands; proposes postponing appropriations and reducing expenditures during the depression.

sources.title: Inaugural Address, March 4, 1837
sources.author: Martin Van Buren, via Miller Center
sources.usedFor: Strict construction, powers left to the States, popular government, strict neutrality and no meddling in other countries' disputes, slavery pledge.

sources.title: Roll calls of Senator Martin Van Buren, 20th Congress (1828 tariff bill): votes 90-96, 138-140
sources.author: Voteview, UCLA (Lewis et al.), US Senate roll calls
sources.usedFor: Voted yes on duty increases on woolens and ready-made clothing and yes to pass the 1828 tariff bill (vote checked in the local Voteview dataset).

sources.title: The Autobiography of Martin Van Buren (AHA 1918)
sources.author: Martin Van Buren, ed. John C. Fitzpatrick
sources.library: Martin Van Buren - The Autobiography of Martin Van Buren (AHA 1918).txt
sources.usedFor: His account of the 1821 New York suffrage debate (reform step by step), the 1833 report against nullification that he wrote, and his 1832-33 work for a settlement of the tariff grievances.

sources.title: Martin Van Buren: Domestic Affairs
sources.author: Mark Cheathem, Miller Center
sources.usedFor: Independent Treasury, rejection of a national bank, enforcement of Cherokee removal, Amistad, Texas, slavery policy.

sources.title: Martin Van Buren: Life After the Presidency
sources.author: Mark Cheathem, Miller Center
sources.usedFor: Opposition to immediate Texas annexation (1844), Free Soil nomination (1848), and his support for Lincoln and the Union war effort in 1861.

sources.title: Inquiry into the Origin and Course of Political Parties in the United States (1867)
sources.author: Martin Van Buren
sources.usedFor: His late-life account of the three departments as coordinate and independent, the moneyed power Hamilton built around the Bank, and Jefferson's Virginia reforms (religious freedom, abolition of entail and primogeniture) as indispensable to republican government.

notes: Themes searched: economy (bank, Independent Treasury, deficits, tariff, public lands), government (constitutional limits, federalism, secession, executive patronage), society (slavery, suffrage, Indian removal, religion), world (neutrality, Canada, Texas, navy and militia). All four annual or special messages, the inaugural and the Canadian messages in the Miller Center collection, his Autobiography (local library copy) and his posthumous Inquiry into the Origin and Course of Political Parties (archive.org, inquiryintoorigi00vanb) were downloaded and searched; the Inquiry and Miller Center essays are kept in scratchpad/sources/martin-van-buren/. Also searched the full statement list (598 statements) against his messages, the Autobiography and the Inquiry. Left null because the record fits either answer: Texas non-annexation (declined for the sake of the Union and the economy, not stated as opposition to expansion), the March 1840 ten-hour order for federal public works (not a statement on unions or wages), the Amistad handover as reported by Cheathem, the Independent Treasury (no statement on central banking as such), the public land preemption and graduation policy (no stated view on widely distributed property), and Dred Scott, which the Inquiry endorses as correct on the citizenship of Black Americans. His 1837 slavery pledge (veto any bill abolishing slavery in the District of Columbia against the slaveholding States' wishes and resist interference in the States) matches no statement in the bank. The Inquiry criticizes the protective system, his 1828 votes are the record and answer the tariff statement alone. His 1848 Free Soil nomination and the earlier proslavery record differ, and no statement settles either. The record is thin on ecology, technology, culture, family and most liberty statements; failing the uncertainty rule is the expected honest result. Foreign-affairs essay (Cheathem, millercenter.org/president/vanburen/foreign-affairs) read: he enforced neutrality toward the Canadian rebellions and settled the Aroostook dispute peacefully, which fits either answer on intervention. Religion, family and women, class and race themes were searched in the messages, the Autobiography and the Inquiry beyond the answers recorded (the Autobiography's account of the Cherokee missionaries and the Inquiry's Dred Scott chapter were read); no further stated position settles a statement, so lines for secularism, family, class and race stay thin.
